To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the scaling of plant species richness from the level of individuals to the level of a province is consistent across three species‐rich temperate grasslands, but that the scaling is strongly affected by the number of individuals sampled at the level of individuals.

the spatial scaling of plant species richness is similar at the scale of an individual to that of an ecological province, and that this similarity is revealed by the integration of local and regional species‐area relationships from space‐time species accumulation.

(1) species‐rich grassland communities are characterized by species accumulation over space and time, (2) the rate of species accumulation is highly constrained by sampling at small scales but is consistent with the spatial scaling of larger‐scale species‐richness estimates once the sampling constraint is removed, and (3) the spatial scaling of sampling‐corrected fine‐scale species richness is consistent with the scaling of larger‐floristic‐province species richness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the integration of local and regional species‐area curves and the decoupling of ecological from sampling processes.
the scaling of biodiversity from small to large spatial scales.
how to remove the sampling constraint from species‐area curves to better understand the ecological processes that determine the scaling of species diversity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spatial scaling of local species richness is consistent with the spatial scaling of regional richness.

the scaling of plant species richness from the scale of an individual to that of an ecological region is consistent with the scaling of species‐area curves from space and from time, and is consistent across three regions of very different sizes and compositions.

the scaling of local richness curves is largely determined by the sampling constraint, and that this constraint can be removed to yield species‐area relationships that reflect the ecological processes of the larger regions in which they occur.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the species richness of a region is the sum of its local species richnesses, but that the local richnesses are not independent of each other.
species‐area curves for local communities are not simply scaled‐up versions of regional ones, but that the scaling of richness at the local scale is consistent with that at the regional scale.
the species‐area curve for a given area is the sum of the species‐area curves of its constituent parts.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the species‐area relationship, which has long been considered an important tool for understanding the ecological causes and consequences of species richness, can be applied across scales, even to the smallest areas, provided that sampling processes are taken into account.

the spatial scaling of plant diversity may be more consistent than previously thought, and that sampling processes, rather than environmental heterogeneity, may be the primary determinant of fine‐scale species richness.
the spatial scaling of plant species richness is a consistent property of plant communities that emerges from the interactions of ecological and sampling processes across scales.
